Related to this, when we move scripts across documents, the following things (associated with Document) are not changed and thus, for example, set-of-scripts-that-will-execute-as-soon-as-possible of Document A can contain script elements that now belongs to another Document B, right?

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#list-of-scripts-that-will-execute-when-the-document-has-finished-parsing
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#list-of-scripts-that-will-execute-in-order-as-soon-as-possible
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#set-of-scripts-that-will-execute-as-soon-as-possible
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#pending-parsing-blocking-script

Also we might want to update the following non-normative notes:
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#pending-parsing-blocking-script
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-execution-of-scripts-that-are-moving-across-multiple-documents

In general let me know what you think. I am not 100% confident in my interpretation of when we should fire the error event, but I think the latest is pretty good. Happy to hear your thoughts.

> Related to this, when we move scripts across documents, the following things (associated with Document) are not changed and thus, for example, set-of-scripts-that-will-execute-as-soon-as-possible of Document A can contain script elements that now belongs to another Document B, right?

I looked into these, and most of them are not a problem. The lists will indeed contain scripts from the other document, but that's OK, it just means when we go to execute them, we do nothing.

The pending parsing-blocking script is trickier, and I am not sure if maybe it is a problem. It seems like it might be OK to leave the spec as-is, and let it continue blocking until it is ready to execute, even though if it gets moved elsewhere, executing will be a no-op. What do you think?

> Also we might want to update the following non-normative notes: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#pending-parsing-blocking-script

If we go with the above (no change), then I think this note is still accurate.

> https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-execution-of-scripts-that-are-moving-across-multiple-documents

This section seems to match the new spec text, but not match the old spec text, which is interesting. Did you have any change in mind?

Talked with @hiroshige-g in person to help me page all this back into my head. Things to do:

- When moving between documents, we have two reasonable choices:
  - The error/load event fires, depending on what happens on the network
  - Neither event fires, no matter what happens on the network
  
  Right now the PR is in a bad in-between state where if the network request succeeds, the load event fires, but if it fails, the error event does not fire.

  We prefer suppressing the events since the whole point here is to not run script, so it's a better conservative default.
- About the pending parser-blocking stuff, the PR's approach is good; it avoids having to do something at the time something is moved. But we do need to update the non-normative note, which currently says "at which time the script executes"; it should be "at which time the run a script algorithm runs (and immediately does nothing)" or similar.
- This may work better on top of #2991.

@hiroshige-g This should work better now; would love your review here and on https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/pull/5911 . I think our plan is still to not merge the spec change until we have shown this is web-compatible. However we can merge the test changes with a .tentative.html extension if that helps Blink's implementation.

BTW given results at https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/pull/5911#issuecomment-301188437 I am not sure why I wanted to wait on Chrome before merging this. Roughly matching 2/4 browsers with a better behavior seems pretty reasonable, especially given Chrome's expressed _interest_ in aligning with this spec change.

> Nobody has ever discussed changing the object's relevant realm (i.e. creation realm)

I'm pretty sure that's what Gecko does on adoption, @bzbarsky can correct me. If it didn't it'd still leak the old realm and the goal of changing the prototype and such on adoption is to not leak that.
In #3486 you state this would also fix that, but my results (note that I'm not testing the parser) have three browsers stacked against Firefox (and I haven't really tested external scripts yet).
So I think we could still merge this and then have additional fixes for #3486 on top. But maybe you want to get the full story fixed first?
I think I would prefer the full story since when we ask implementers to make changes it's better to have a full accounting of the changes we are asking them to make.

If that's the case I hope you can take over this PR and tests; I've done my best to converge on a behavior that has multi-implementer support, but I don't have time to do the full archeology here.

I'd still prefer landing this as a series of well-layered changes.

@annevk Chrome would like to ship this soon, at which point we would have 3/4 browsers matching this change. As I stated previously I would prefer to land this and then someone can work on #3486 on top of it. Do you still object to aligning with 3/4 browsers?

@cdumez any interest in aligning Safari on this?

Intent to deprecate&remove is sent out to change the Chromium's behavior:
https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/d/topic/blink-dev/KyB2mwOmjrk/discussion

Filed a Safari issue https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=202714.

> @annevk Chrome would like to ship this soon, at which point we would have 3/4 browsers matching this change. As I stated previously I would prefer to land this and then someone can work on #3486 on top of it. Do you still object to aligning with 3/4 browsers?
> 
> @cdumez any interest in aligning Safari on this?

Yes, this seems like a good idea and I think WebKit should align. Sorry I missed this GitHub notification earlier.

Revisiting this to get it cleaned up as Blink prepares to change their behavior. @hiroshige, can you review the latest patch set and let me know if there are any outstanding issues besides the one below? Also, can you point ot the latest web platform tests---I think you probably have some that supercede my https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/5911 ?

> Are there any observable cases where the element's node document is not equal to the node document at the time of prepare a script but the script is evaluated?
>
> In other words, are the conditions (relevant settings object check + scripting is disabled check) equivalent to the node document check + scripting is disabled check?
>
> node document check: If the element's node document here (i.e. at the time of execute a script block) is not equal to the node document at the time of prepare a script, then return.

These are equivalent. It is just a matter of reusing the spec's preexisting "the script's script's settings object" field, versus adding a new "the script's original document" field.

> These are equivalent. It is just a matter of reusing the spec's preexisting "the script's script's settings object" field, versus adding a new "the script's original document" field.

Thanks for clarification. Adding a note might be helpful for justifying implementations that checks Document identity instead of settings object (Chromium implementation will check the element document and context document).
As for WPT, I was drafting https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/19632 to try the current behavior for failed loading (but blocked because WPT bots didn't run as commented there).

Updated the WPT PR (https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/19632).
Recap of the current behaviors according to the [test bots](https://wpt.fyi/results/html/semantics/scripting-1/the-script-element/moving-between-documents.html?sha=bc8c7eb926&label=pr_head):

- Scripts moved during parsing
    - Executed on Chromium/Safari and not on Firefox, but anyway out of scope of this spec PR.
- Classic scripts moved to documents where scripts aren't forbidden
    - Safari executes such scripts ([bug](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=202714))
    - Chromium stopped executing recently ([bug](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=721914))
    - Firefox doesn't execute since before
- In other cases scripts are not executed when moved across document on Chromium/Safari/Firefox.
- Error/load events behave quite differently.

Thanks so much for working on the WPT PR. Those are very helpful and comprehensive.

Looking at the results, it seems like the error event semantics we came up with in this PR are quite bad. We could have picked Chrome behavior, of no error events in all cases. Or we could have picked the Firefox behavior, of error events in almost all cases. (No error events if moved during parsing, I guess?) Instead we picked only some cases, which matches nobody.

I am sorry for continuing to drag out this PR but I'd like to match at least one browser. I think Chrome is the best choice because it fires error events in no cases. Firefox is almost consistent, but does not fire error events for moving during parsing, so it is not totally consistent and thus a less good choice. And Safari seems very inconsistent.

So I will try to fix up the spec so that it never fires error events for the cases you test, aligning with Chrome. I guess this might be hard since we got stuck before, but I will try my best!!

Again, thank you for the comprehensive tests. Without them this would be much less clear.
Just so I understand the proposed error event semantics, what are the cases that would not fire error events, exactly?

> error events for moving during parsing

These tests are for inline scripts, and inline scripts don't fire `<script>` error event in the first place.

(Er... should we test scripts with *parse* errors moved between documents firing `window` error events or not? This is not tested but perhaps we should...)

> Just so I understand the proposed error event semantics, what are the cases that would not fire error events, exactly?

My proposal is that cases where we would have reason to not execute do not fire error events---even if there was a fetching error for the script. This encompasses:

- scripting being disabled
- parser/prepare-time document mismatches (Gecko/spec-only for now)
- parser/execution-time document mismatches (Gecko/spec-only for now)
- prepare-time document/execution-time document mismatches

But, since as @hiroshige-g points out my reading of the data was a bit incorrect, I'm not 100% sure on this proposal anymore. It seems reasonable still but no longer obviously correct.

> These tests are for inline scripts, and inline scripts don't fire `<script>` error event in the first place.

Oh, hmm, OK. Can we add external script tests? It seems like it should be testable...

Also we should probably test both parser/prepare-time and parser/execution-time document mismatches, if possible. See the last commit on https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/5154.

> (Er... should we test scripts with parse errors moved between documents firing window error events or not? This is not tested but perhaps we should...)

Yeah, that would be good to test. They should not fire such events, per the current spec infrastructure, since we bail out at an earlier step...

---

BTW after the cleanup in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/5154 I think it will be pretty easy to get whichever error event behavior we want, if we can make a decision.

> Also we should probably test both parser/prepare-time and parser/execution-time document mismatches, if possible. See the last commit on #5154.

Nevermind. This is redundant since we have tests for both parser/prepare-time and prepare-time/execution-time.

> Nevermind. This is redundant since we have tests for both parser/prepare-time and prepare-time/execution-time.

No, wait, it is not redundant, I think... The question is whether we fetch the script or not if there's a parser/prepare-time mismatch. I.e. we'd need to test whether the server gets hit. Anyway, this is all more about #2137...

This PR is now rebased on top of the editorial work in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/5154 which should make it much easier to review, if you look only at the new commit. (Currently that commit is https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2673/commits/29cd353acc2a3d02a2c74b293295f341f1c41fb6.) It becomes a one-line insertion. And we could easily change it from "return" to "fire an error event then return".

Updated [tests](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/19632) and [results](https://wpt.fyi/results/html/semantics/scripting-1/the-script-element/moving-between-documents?sha=7d0614ddd4&label=pr_head).

- When `preparation-time document` != `node's document` at the time of `#execute-the-script-block`: (see after-prepare-* tests)
  - Firefox: Fires `<script>`'s error events in all external script cases.
  - Chromium: No evaluation && no events (recently changed behavior).
  - Safari: Fires Window's error events for successful module scripts.
    In other cases, evaluating/firing events as normal.

- When `parser document` != `preparation-time document` at `#prepare-a-script`: (see before-prepare-* tests; #2137)
  - Current spec: No evaluation && no events.
  - Firefox: No evaluation && no events.
  - Chromium and Safari: evaluating/firing events as normal.

Note on Safari's behavior (probably not related to moving between Documents):
- Parse errors in module scripts seem to fire `<script>` error events instead of window error events.
- Transfer-encoding errors seem to be handled differently from ordinal fetch errors like 404.
Edited the OP with Firefox and Safari bugs. Yay!
